Sir Galahad
Alfred, Lord Tennyson, 1842
[Omitted: the first four stanzas]
When down the stormy crescent goes, A light before me swims, Between dark stems the forest glows, I hear a noise of hymns: Then by some secret shrine I ride; I hear a voice, but none are there; The stalls are void, the doors are wide, The tapers burning fair. Fair gleams the snowy altar-cloth, The silver vessels sparkle clean, The shrill bell rings, the censer swings, And solemn chaunts resound between.
[Omitted: the stanzas that follow]
stormy crescent: the thin moon going down through storm clouds · stems: tree trunks · shrine: a small holy place · stalls: the carved seats in a chapel · void: empty · tapers: thin candles · censer: a hanging pot that burns sweet incense · chaunts: chants, sung prayers
Text: The Early Poems of Alfred Lord Tennyson, ed. John Churton Collins (Methuen, 1900), Project Gutenberg #8601. Public domain.

🍎 At the Board with Professor Lovelore
Simple, compound, and complex sentences
Professor Lovelore At the board
1:15
An AI-generated character and voice.
Simple
one complete thought
Galahad took the seat.
Compound
two complete thoughts, a comma, and a joining word
and · but · or · so · for · nor · yet
Galahad took the seat, and the knights wondered.
Complex
a complete thought and a part that cannot stand alone
because · when · although · before
When the cloth was drawn away, the knights saw the new letters.
1. Equal partners
and · but · so join two equal thoughts.
Each half could stand alone.
2. The leaning part
because · when · although make one part lean on the other.
Because the Grail was veiled: not a sentence by itself.
3. Comma after it
When the leaning part comes first,
put a comma after it.
2
✏️ Grammar: Learn
Step 1 of 3 this week: sentence types and the words that join them.

A simple sentence is one complete thought. A compound sentence joins two complete thoughts. A complex sentence joins a complete thought to a part that leans on it.

TypeWhat it isExample
simpleone complete thoughtGalahad took the seat.
compoundtwo complete thoughts joined by a comma and a joining word; each half could stand aloneGalahad took the seat, and the knights wondered.
complexa complete thought and a part that cannot stand aloneWhen the cloth was drawn away, the knights saw the new letters.
the comma rulewhen the leaning part comes first, a comma follows itBecause the Grail was veiled, the knights could not see it.
The joining wordsThey are
join two equal thoughts (compound)and, but, or, so, for, nor, yet
make a part lean (complex)because, when, although, before, after, since, while

📌 Watch how
Tobias’s paragraph
6th Grade Scholar

Sir Bors shows that a good knight can serve the quest even when the glory goes to someone else. When Galahad sits in the Siege Perilous and lives, Bors cries out, “Upon pain of my life, this young knight shall achieve great things!” (Chapter 1). He praises the young knight in front of the whole court, and he does not ask for anything for himself. At Carbonek, Bors eats only bread and drinks clear water, and he kneels at King Pelles’s side while the Grail is brought (Chapter 7). Green says Bors “had seen all these things,” so he becomes the quest’s witness. Although Galahad is the one who achieves the Grail, Bors does a job no one else can do. He rides back to Camelot and tells the whole tale, because the court needs to know what happened. A good knight, Green suggests, stays faithful when the brightest honor belongs to someone else.
